Under Mill's principle of liberty, someone may forcibly stop a person who is about to cross a bridge known to be unsafe, as stated in [1] and [2]. Force is allowed when there is a certainty of harm, such as in the case of the unsafe bridge, where the person does not desire to fall into the river. On the other hand, when there is only a danger of mischief, but not a certainty, the person should only be warned of the danger, not forcibly prevented from exposing himself to it, as explained in [2]. This does not breach his liberty because liberty consists in doing what one desires, and the person does not desire to fall into the river. According to [3], the principle of liberty does not apply to children, or to young persons below the age of manhood or womanhood, as they are still in a state to require being taken care of by others and must be protected against their own actions.

On the Origin of Species (1st edition, 1859): The elephant is reckoned to be the slowest breeder of all known animals, and it breeds when thirty years old, and goes on breeding till ninety years old, bringing forth three pair of young in this interval; if this be so, at the end of the fifth century there would be alive fifteen million elephants, descended from the first pair.
On the Origin of Species (6th edition, 1872): The elephant is reckoned the slowest breeder of all known animals, and it begins breeding when thirty years old, and goes on breeding till ninety years old, bringing forth six young in the interval, and surviving till one hundred years old; if this be so, after a period of from 740 to 750 years there would be nearly nineteen million elephants alive descended from the first pair.
Darwin's assumptions changed from three pair of young to six young, and the time interval for the result changed from the end of the fifth century to 740 to 750 years, with the result changing from fifteen million to nineteen million elephants.

Darwin describes the struggle for existence as the doctrine of Malthus applied to the whole animal and vegetable kingdoms. According to Malthus' essay, population increases in a geometrical ratio, while subsistence increases only in an arithmetical ratio, as stated in [1] and [10]. Malthus takes a doubling period of twenty-five years as his rule for unchecked population, as mentioned in [2] and [14]. This implies a strong and constantly operating check on population from the difficulty of subsistence, as stated in [11]. The power of population is indefinitely greater than the power in the earth to produce subsistence for man, as stated in [10].

On Liberty by John Stuart Mill: Mill sees the tyranny of the majority as reaching into the "details of life, and enslaving the soul itself" through the imposition of its own ideas and practices as rules of conduct on those who dissent.
Democracy in America by Tocqueville: Tocqueville sees the tyranny of the majority as affecting "the manners than in the conduct of society" and checking "the development of leading characters".
The values are not directly comparable as they describe the reach of the tyranny of the majority in different aspects of society.
